name: Sleep on your back (anti-wrinkle)

lead: Sleeping on your back keeps your face off the pillow, so the skin isn't compressed and folded night after night. People do it to avoid sleep lines and keep the face smoother over time.

Appearance communities promote it, and encyclopedic sources list habitual sleeping position among factors in skin wrinkles alongside aging, sun damage and facial expressions. The support cited is general educational material; no trial of sleep position and wrinkles was found.

paras: People train themselves to sleep supine, sometimes using pillows to hold the position, and often pair it with a silk pillowcase or a thin pillow. Visible changes are judged over months.
Back sleeping is associated with more sleep apnea, reflux and sleep paralysis in some people, so those prone to these may do better on their side.

web.title: Researchers review wrinkles occurring through facial compression during sleep - Healio

angle.text: Sleeping face-up keeps the skin from being folded against a pillow night after night, aiming to prevent sleep lines. Sleeping position is listed among wrinkle factors in reference sources, though no trial has tested the habit.

lead: Sleeping on the back is promoted in skincare and looksmaxxing circles as a free way to avoid 'sleep lines' and one-sided facial compression. The idea is that a face lying flat is not pressed into a pillow for hours each night, so skin is not folded or pushed in the same place repeatedly.[1][2]

A 2016 literature review in Aesthetic Surgery Journal, led by plastic surgeon Goesel Anson, argued that facial tissue is pushed, pulled and compressed during side or stomach sleeping, that sleep wrinkles differ from expression wrinkles in origin, location and direction, and that avoiding facial distortion, for example by back sleeping, is the reliable way to minimise them.[2] The authors acknowledged that changing sleep habits is difficult and called for more study.[2]

Wikipedia lists habitual sleeping position among factors contributing to skin wrinkles, alongside aging, sun damage and facial expressions.[1] Back sleeping also has health associations, including more positional sleep apnea and reflux in some people.[3] On looksmax.org, members debate whether side sleeping changes facial symmetry or wrinkles and how to learn to sleep supine.[4][5]
infobox: Fewer sleep lines and less one-sided compression

paras: The practice involves sleeping supine, sometimes with a pillow arrangement to keep the face off the bed. The Wikipedia article on wrinkles names habitual sleeping position as a contributing factor and points to a dermatology educational page.[1]

Healio's report on the 2016 review says the authors described sleep wrinkles as forming where skin buckles under external pressure, with habitual sleep patterns able to reinforce expression lines, and noted that specialty pillows designed to reduce facial distortion exist.[2]

The 2016 review examined how wrinkles develop from intrinsic and extrinsic influences, concluding that shear, compression and tension forces act on facial tissue during side or stomach sleeping, and that these forces may contribute to facial aging because of the many hours spent asleep.[2] The lead author disclosed a partnership with a company selling a sleep-wrinkle pillow, and the review is a literature analysis rather than a trial.[2]

A looksmax.org thread on side versus back sleeping states that side sleeping contributes at most slightly to asymmetry, that only a few studies suggest it might lead to wrinkles or droopier eyelids over time, and that bone structure is not meaningfully changed by sleeping on one side.[4]
Supine sleeping is linked to more positional obstructive sleep apnea, sleep paralysis and reflux when lying flat after eating, and side sleeping is the most common adult position.[3]
Forum members share ways to sleep supine, including a thread recommending a hammock, which drew replies about spinal support.[5] A Hacker News thread asked how to learn to sleep on the back.[6]

No studies found comparing sleeping positions to wrinkle formation in controlled trials. The 2016 Aesthetic Surgery Journal literature review discusses the mechanical forces on the face during sleep.[2]
